candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the apostles' petition 'Lord, increase our faith' (Lk 17:5), Cyril reads the prosthes-hēmin-pistin (add-to-us-faith) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that faith is a gift to be asked for, not a quality to be produced: the apostles do not say 'we will work harder' but 'Lord, give us more'. Christ's mustard-seed answer (Lk 17:6) does not rebuke the request but redirects it — faith's POWER is not in its quantity but in its OBJECT (God's omnipotence). Tewahedo faith-formation cites Lk 17:5 + Lk 17:6 as the canonical doubled-Lukan-witness that faith is request-receivable from God (not striven-produced by self) and small-but-real-faith is sufficient if its object is the true God.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do' (Lk 17:10), Cyril reads the unprofitable-servants-formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of grace-against-merit: even maximal Christian-virtuous-action puts the disciple no further than baseline-duty; salvation is never owed to the disciple. The Greek achreioi (unprofitable, but also 'without-superfluous-claim') captures the disposition of the just-debtor with no surplus. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 17:10 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the monk's perpetual-humility-formula — 'I am an unprofitable servant' is recited in the daily-office.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

Only the Samaritan among the ten cleansed lepers returns to give thanks at Christ's feet, and Cyril reads the verse as the canonical Lukan anchor of the eucharistic posture: the cleansed turn back to the cleanser in thanksgiving (eucharistia). The nine who do not return are not cured of the deeper leprosy of ingratitude. Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the Cyrillian reading: the proper response to divine cleansing is the return-to-the-altar with thanks.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mk 1:15.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'the kingdom of God is within you' (Lk 17:21 — entos hymōn estin), Cyril reads the entos-hymōn (within-you or among-you) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the present-immanent-kingdom: in Christ's person and ministry, the kingdom has already arrived among the questioners — the Pharisees see-but-do-not-recognize it. Cyril allows both readings (within = interior reign of God in the believer; among = Christ-the-kingdom-present-among). The Greek is deliberately ambiguous.
